steps.body: **Perpendicular lines** cross at exactly 90° — a right angle, the same benchmark from Course 9. Diagrams mark the crossing with a small square symbol, not an arrow. A plus sign (+) is the classic perpendicular shape.
Construct perpendicular lines and show that the right angle stays the same.

widget.prompt: Rotate the active blue line until it is perpendicular to the dark line, then translate it and confirm the 90° crossing survives.
widget.successFeedback: Perpendicular: the lines cross at exactly 90°, even after translation.
widget.angleFeedback: Crossing is not enough. Rotate until the smallest intersection angle is exactly 90°.
widget.distanceFeedback: Move both controls so you can distinguish changing angle from changing position.

predict.reveal: Perpendicular is a special crossing — exactly 90°, a perfect square corner. Lines can cross at a thousand other angles and earn no badge for it.

cml.actionGoal: Construct a 90-degree line relation and test translation as a counterfactual.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Translate after reaching the target relation. Which invariant survives, and which measurements change?

explanation.prompt: What changes when you translate instead of rotate?

options.label: Position changes while direction stays fixed.
options.feedback: Exactly — that separates translation from rotation.

options.label: Direction must change too.
options.feedback: Direction changes only when the line rotates.

explanationVariants: Perpendicular means crossing at exactly 90° — nothing more, nothing less.
The exact right-angle crossing is the whole definition.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross, forming a perfect right angle. What are they?

options.label: Perpendicular lines
options.feedback: Crossing at exactly 90° is the definition of perpendicular.

options.label: Parallel lines
options.feedback: Parallel lines NEVER cross. These lines DO cross, and at a right angle — that makes them perpendicular.

options.label: Intersecting lines only
options.feedback: All perpendicular lines do intersect, but 'intersecting' alone doesn't require a right angle. The right-angle crossing makes these specifically perpendicular.

options.label: Rays
options.feedback: A ray is about one endpoint and one direction — it isn't a relationship between two crossing lines. A 90° crossing is perpendicular.

steps.body: The word **'exactly'** matters, just like Course 9's angle boundaries. Two lines crossing at 89° are close, but not perpendicular — only a true 90° crossing counts. 'Almost perpendicular' isn't a real category.

explanationVariants: 89° falls short of the exact 90° needed — these lines are just crossing, not perpendicular.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross at 89°. Are they perpendicular?

options.label: They aren't — perpendicular requires exactly 90°
options.feedback: 89° is close, but perpendicular means EXACTLY 90° — one degree off disqualifies it.

options.label: Yes — 89° is basically 90°
options.feedback: Perpendicular has no 'basically' — it means exactly 90°. At 89°, these lines are just crossing.

options.label: Yes, since it's so close
options.feedback: Closeness doesn't count here, the same way 89° wasn't 'almost a right angle' back in Course 9. Perpendicular requires exactly 90°.

options.label: It depends on how the lines are drawn
options.feedback: The angle measure alone decides it: 89° is not 90°, so these lines are not perpendicular.

widget.prompt: Sort each example: perpendicular, or just crossing?

items.label: A flagpole meeting flat ground
items.feedback: An upright flagpole meets flat ground at exactly 90° — perpendicular.

items.label: A leaning ladder against a wall
items.feedback: A leaning ladder meets the ground at an angle other than 90° — just crossing.

items.label: The corner of a book page
items.feedback: A standard book page's corner is a right angle — perpendicular.

items.label: Two branches meeting at a Y-shape
items.feedback: A Y-shape's branches typically meet at an angle other than 90° — just crossing.

widget.missFeedback: Ask whether the crossing forms an exact right angle, or some other angle.
widget.successFeedback: The flagpole and book corner cross at exactly 90°; the leaning ladder and Y-branches don't.

explanationVariants: A small square symbol at a crossing is the standard mark for a right angle — perpendicular.
That symbol specifically means 90°, nothing else.

widget.prompt: A diagram marks a crossing point with a small square symbol. What does this indicate?

options.label: The lines are perpendicular, crossing at 90°
options.feedback: The small square is the standard symbol for a right angle — perpendicular lines.

options.label: The lines are parallel
options.feedback: Parallel lines don't cross at all, so there's no crossing point to mark. The square marks a 90° crossing: perpendicular.

options.label: The lines form some angle less than 90°
options.feedback: The square symbol specifically means EXACTLY 90°, not just any angle under 90°.

options.label: The figure is a specific shape, like a square
options.feedback: The small square at a crossing is a symbol for the ANGLE there, not a claim about the whole figure's shape.

hints: A well-built bookshelf has vertical sides meeting a flat, level shelf.
Check the crossing angle where the side meets the shelf.
A properly built shelf meets its side at exactly 90°.
explanationVariants: A properly built bookshelf's vertical side meets its level shelf at exactly 90° — perpendicular.
The exact right-angle crossing is what makes a shelf sit flat and sturdy.

widget.prompt: A bookshelf's vertical side meets its flat, level shelf at exactly 90°. What is this relationship called?

options.label: Perpendicular
options.feedback: An exact 90° crossing between the side and shelf is perpendicular.

options.label: Parallel
options.feedback: Parallel lines never cross — but the side and shelf clearly meet. A 90° crossing makes them perpendicular.

options.label: Just crossing, since any two boards that meet do so at some angle
options.feedback: The specific 90° angle described here is exactly what makes it perpendicular, not merely 'crossing at some angle.'

options.label: It depends on the bookshelf's overall size
options.feedback: Size doesn't matter here — the 90° crossing angle is what determines perpendicular, regardless of the shelf's dimensions.

takeaways: Perpendicular lines cross at exactly 90° — the same right-angle benchmark from Course 9.
A small square symbol marks a perpendicular crossing in diagrams.
89° or 91° isn't 'close enough' — only an exact 90° crossing counts.
steps.teaser: next: spotting both parallel and perpendicular pairs in one figure.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Perpendicular means crossing at exactly 90°.** A plus sign (+) is the clearest example — its two strokes cross at a perfect right angle, marked with a small square symbol in diagrams.

explanationVariants: A plus sign's strokes cross at exactly 90° — perpendicular.
The right-angle crossing is the definition.

widget.prompt: The two strokes of a plus sign (+) cross at exactly 90°. What is this relationship?

options.label: Perpendicular
options.feedback: Exactly 90° is perpendicular.

options.label: Parallel
options.feedback: Parallel lines never cross at all. These clearly do, at exactly 90° — perpendicular.

options.label: Just an estimate
options.feedback: A plus sign's crossing is precisely 90°, not just an estimate — that makes it perpendicular.
